products.section_lead: Buy capacity into the network from your stop — or help anchor a trunk that makes your waterfront launch.

items.title: N30 Executive Shuttle
items.body: Start small: on-demand or pilot seats for leadership pods and early adopters — then grow into scheduled network capacity at your terminal.

items.title: N45 Commuter Line
items.body: Twenty seats. Scheduled corridor service when a line has enough committed seats. Built for campus-scale commute benefits — not a one-off charter.

seats.title: Option A — Reserve seats
seats.body: Signal interest in seats for your team on a line. Non-binding. Helps us sequence launch order.

anchor.title: Option B — Anchor a line
anchor.body: Underwrite a vessel, brand the service, and help shape the service window for a full line.

copy.hero_headline: One terminal. The whole Bay network.
copy.hero_sub: Electric hydrofoil commutes that meet at transfer hubs. Your campus only needs a stop on the water — employees board near home, transfer once if needed, and arrive at your door.
copy.stripe_lesson: In 2024 we ran the first employer water commute on the Bay — daily service for Stripe employees, North Bay to Oyster Point. The ride delivered. The open lesson: mass commute needs our twenty-seat vessel, not an eight-seat executive craft. The ride worked. The vessel class is what we fixed.
copy.loi_cta: Non-binding. Helps us sequence lines to real demand at your terminal — and every origin that can transfer to you.
copy.price_anchor: roughly a parking space — often less

problem_chips.label: Often cut rush-hour time on flagship water routes
Your campus plugs into the full network

copy.launch_trigger: A line advances when about 60–80 seats are committed on that corridor — enough for real commuter service.
copy.problem_title: The bridge is the bottleneck. The Bay is the spare lane.
copy.problem_lead: Your people already live and work on water-adjacent campuses. Rush-hour road time is the tax. Water cuts that tax — quietly, on a service window you help form with seat interest.
copy.proof_lead: The Stripe pilot is public record. The lesson was the vessel class — not the water.
copy.proof_worked_body: Smooth, quiet, daily employer commute on the water.
copy.proof_fixed_body: Commuter economics need the twenty-seat vessel, not an eight-seat executive shuttle.
copy.proof_ask_body: Non-binding seat interest so we light the right line first.
copy.network_lead: Pick where your people live and where you work. We’ll show the water path — including transfers — and compare it to a typical AM peak drive. Gold rings are transfer hubs.
copy.map_detail_empty: Pick two terminals in Find my ride — or select a line or stop.
copy.calc_lead_html: Optional planning math. If you ran Find my ride, water and drive times are prefilled from that route. Defaults reproduce a worked example of $4,500/mo net incremental — about $75 per rider.
copy.hero_note: Non-binding letter of intent · no commitment · helps us sequence which line launches first
copy.hero_cta_network: Find a route to my office
copy.network_footnote: Gold rings mark transfer hubs (Ferry Building, Mission Bay, Oyster Point, Oakland JLS). Stops are usable marina/pier berths — not all are traditional ferry terminals. You don’t sponsor every line — riders transfer to your stop.
copy.office_lead: You don’t need a stop on every line. Sit on a hub — or any stop that feeds one — and riders transfer to you. Tap a campus to set it as your office and see who can reach you at launch vs full network.
copy.office_insight: Example: an LOI at Oyster Point still serves Marin and East Bay riders who transfer at the Ferry Building. One location, network leverage.
copy.why_lead: The bridge is the bottleneck. The Bay is the spare lane — terminal to terminal, above the traffic.
